question: Let $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}p & q \\ p & q\end{bmatrix},$$ where $p$ and $q$ are not both zero. Show that $AB=O$. What does this example establish?
explanation:
Multiplication of the matrices
$$AB=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p & q \\ p & q\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}p-p & q-q \\ 2p-2p & 2q-2q\end{bmatrix}$$
Therefore, $$AB=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}=O$$
Non-zero factors
$A$ is non-zero, and since $p$ and $q$ are not both zero, $B$ is also non-zero.
Conclusion
This establishes that $AB=O$ does not necessarily imply $A=O$ or $B=O$.

options.A: $AB=\begin{bmatrix}p&q\\2p&2q\end{bmatrix}$, so $AB\ne O$ whenever $p$ or $q$ is non-zero.
options.C: $AB=O$ even though both factors are non-zero; thus $AB=O$ need not imply $A=O$ or $B=O$.
